sysd-found-032.title: HTTP: the request and response behind every web page
sysd-found-032.text:
A browser asks for a page, and a server sends one back. That exchange is HTTP, the foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web. It is a stateless, application-layer request-response protocol that clients and servers use to exchange hypertext and other content.

HTTP lives in the client-server model. The client sends a request, and the server returns a response that describes the outcome and may carry a resource such as an HTML document. A web browser is the usual client and a web server the usual server. Other user agents include voice browsers and mobile apps. A web resource is located by a URL, using the http scheme or, when encrypted, the {{ref:sysd-found-048}} scheme.

HTTP needs a reliable transport underneath. Before HTTP/3 the standard choice is TCP, typically on port 80 when unencrypted and port 443 when encrypted. Because HTTP is stateless, the server is not required to retain information about each user across multiple requests.

Intermediaries such as web caches and proxies can improve or enable communication, and browsers also cache what they fetch to reduce network traffic. Some headers are managed hop by hop by intermediaries, while others are managed end to end, only by the source client and the target web server. RFC 9110 defines the semantics shared by all versions of HTTP, and those semantics are not versioned: methods, status codes and fields mean the same in every version.

sysd-found-173.title: Public-key cryptography: one key to lock, another to open
sysd-found-173.text: A shared secret key has an awkward first step: both sides must get the key, securely, before they can say anything private. Public-key cryptography, or asymmetric cryptography, removes that burden. It uses pairs of related keys, a public key that can be shared openly and a private key that must stay secret. Only private keys need protecting. Anyone with the public key can encrypt a message, but only the private-key holder can decrypt it. That hides the content without telling the recipient who sent it. A digital signature runs the other way. The sender signs with the private key, anyone with the public key can verify it, and a forger cannot make a valid one. The price is speed. Public-key algorithms are far more computationally intensive than symmetric ones, so {{ref:sysd-found-049}}, SSH and PGP are hybrids. A public-key exchange shares a symmetric key, and that key then encrypts the data at higher throughput. The hard part is proving a public key is authentic, because an attacker who swaps in their own key can mount a {{ref:sysd-found-179}}.

sysd-found-033.title: Inside an HTTP message: start line, headers and body
sysd-found-033.text: A request begins with one line such as GET /customer/123 HTTP/1.1. Every HTTP message is a header followed by an optional body: clients send request messages, and servers answer with response messages. A request's start line holds the method name, the request URI and the protocol version. A response's start line holds the protocol version, a status code and optionally a reason phrase, as in HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request. Below it come header fields, name-value pairs separated by a colon that carry metadata about the message. In HTTP/1.1 every request header field except Host is optional, and a field name is matched ignoring case, unlike a method name, which must match exactly. The body may hold data in any format. The format must match the Content-Type header field when the message has one, and the body can be blank. Messages in {{ref:sysd-found-040}} and HTTP/3 are binary, compress headers with HPACK or QPACK, and replace the request or response line with pseudo-header fields.

sysd-found-038.title: Why HTTP reuses one TCP connection for many requests
sysd-found-038.text: In the early web, every resource cost its own TCP connection. HTTP/0.9 always closed the connection after the response and HTTP/1.0 should do so, so each resource needed a new one. A persistent connection lets one TCP connection be reused for more than one HTTP request and response, and HTTP/1.1 officially introduced keep-alive to allow it. Reuse cuts latency, because the client does not repeat the TCP 3-way handshake. The connection also tends to speed up over time because of TCP's slow-start mechanism. HTTP/1.1 added {{ref:sysd-found-170}} too, which lets a client send several requests before waiting for each response. It was never really safe. Some servers and many proxies mishandled it. They served only the first request, closed the connection or returned responses out of order, so it was disabled and then removed from most browsers. Under {{ref:sysd-found-040}}, many concurrent requests and responses are multiplexed through a single TCP/IP connection, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP instead of TCP. Either side can close a connection at any time.

sysd-found-034.title: GET, POST, PUT and the other HTTP request methods
sysd-found-034.text:
The first word of an HTTP request is a verb, and it decides what the request means. The request method, informally a verb, is the primary source of request semantics: it names the action the client wants applied to the target resource.

GET retrieves a current representation of a resource and should only read data. It is the focus of almost all performance optimizations, and its URL can be bookmarked, shared and cached. HEAD is identical to GET except that the server must not send content, so a client can read headers such as Content-Length without transferring the representation.

POST asks the target resource to process the enclosed representation by its own semantics. That covers submitting form data, posting a message or creating a resource, which is reported with 201 (Created) and a Location header. PUT creates or replaces the target resource's state with the state in the request. Unlike POST, the client chooses the target URI, and repeating the same PUT updates the same resource. DELETE removes the association between a resource and its current functionality, like rm in UNIX. PATCH applies a partial modification, saving bandwidth compared with a full PUT.

CONNECT asks a proxy to open a tunnel to the destination server, commonly so TLS can run through it. OPTIONS asks for a resource's communication options, and TRACE loops the request message back for testing and diagnostics. General-purpose servers must support GET and HEAD, and everything else is optional. An unrecognized method should get 501 (Not Implemented), and a known but disallowed one 405 (Method Not Allowed). Responses to GET and HEAD are cacheable. Responses to PUT and DELETE are not.

sysd-found-042.title: Why HTTP forgets you, and how sessions fix that
sysd-found-042.text: A web server may forget you the moment it answers. HTTP is stateless, so it does not require the server to retain information or status about each user across multiple requests. The meaning of each request can be understood on its own, whatever connection it arrives on. That sounds like a handicap, yet many implementations depend on it to reuse proxied connections or to spread requests across multiple servers. A server must also not assume two requests on one connection come from the same user agent. The exception is a connection that is secured and specific to that agent. An application that must remember a user builds a session on top. It implements one with an {{ref:sysd-found-168}}, hidden variables in a web form or another mechanism. A session typically starts with an interactive login and ends with a logout, using a custom mechanism rather than {{ref:sysd-found-043}}.

sysd-found-168.title: How a cookie gives a forgetful protocol a memory
sysd-found-168.text: HTTP forgets you after every response, yet a shop remembers what is in your cart. The memory lives in a cookie: a small block of data that a web server creates and the user's browser stores and sends back. The server sets it with a Set-Cookie response header, and the browser returns it with every request. A cookie is a name and value plus attributes such as expiry, domain and flags. Browsers use the attributes to decide when to delete, block or send the cookie. A session cookie has no Expires or Max-Age and is deleted when the browser closes. A persistent cookie expires at a set date or after a set time and often keeps users logged in. Usually the cookie holds only a unique session identifier, and the server itself keeps the cart or user data. A third-party cookie belongs to a domain other than the one in the address bar. It lets advertisers build a browsing history of a user across every site carrying their content.

sysd-found-037.title: HTTP status codes: five classes of three digits
sysd-found-037.text:
Three digits tell a client how its request went. An HTTP status code is a three-digit number in a response that describes the result of the request and the semantics of the response. Valid codes run from 100 to 599, and the first digit gives the class. Those are informational (100-199), success (200-299), redirection (300-399), client error (400-499) and server error (500-599). The last two digits have no categorization role.

In plain terms, 1xx means the request was received and processing continues, and 2xx that it was accepted. A 3xx says more action is needed. A 4xx says the request is malformed or cannot be fulfilled, and a 5xx that the server failed on a valid-looking request. A single request can have zero or more interim 1xx responses followed by exactly one final response.

Clients are built to cope with codes they do not know. A client must understand the class from the first digit. It treats an unrecognized code as the x00 code of that class, so an unrecognized 471 is handled like 400 (Bad Request). One that receives an invalid status code should treat the response as a 5xx. The reason phrase after the code is only a recommendation and human-readable, while the code is machine-readable.

Some codes are heuristically cacheable, such as 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414 and 501. A cache can reuse those with heuristic expiration unless the method or cache controls say otherwise.

sysd-found-036.title: Idempotent methods: which requests are safe to retry
sysd-found-036.text: If a connection drops before the response arrives, can the client simply send the request again? For some methods it can. A request method is idempotent if the intended effect on the server of several identical requests with it is the same as the effect of one. PUT, DELETE and all {{ref:sysd-found-035}} are idempotent. POST, CONNECT and PATCH are not necessarily, so an identical POST sent twice may modify state again or send two emails. A PUT that sets an email to the value already recorded changes nothing, and deleting an already deleted user has no further effect. A client can repeat an idempotent request automatically after a failure that happens before it reads the response. It should not automatically retry a non-idempotent one unless it knows the request is really idempotent or can detect the original was never applied. A proxy must never do so. Duplicate POSTs can also happen by accident, so it is generally up to the web application to keep a POST from being processed twice.

sysd-found-035.title: Safe methods: requests that only read
sysd-found-035.text: Search spiders can crawl the web without fear of causing harm, thanks to a rule about methods. A request method is safe if its defined semantics are essentially read-only: the client does not request or expect any state change on the origin server. RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as safe, the later QUERY method is also safe, and POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT and PATCH are not. The distinction lets spiders and caches that prefetch work without fear of causing harm. It also lets a user agent warn the user before an unsafe action. A safe method may still have side effects the client did not request and cannot be blamed for, such as appending to an access log. What it must not do is contradict its own semantics. Even if a URI such as page?do=delete suggests an unsafe action, the resource owner must disable it for safe methods. Nothing technically stops a server from changing state on a GET. It is discouraged, because caches, search engines and other automated agents may then make unintended changes.

sysd-found-053.title: Digital certificates: how a browser knows a key is real
sysd-found-053.text: Anyone can claim to be your bank, so a public key by itself proves little. A digital certificate certifies that a named subject owns a public key, and certificate authorities are trusted third parties that sign certificates so others can rely on them. A TLS server certificate holds the server name, the trusted certificate authority that vouches for it, and the server's public key. Trust is anchored in a list of certificates shipped with user agent software such as the browser. To serve a site over {{ref:sysd-found-048}}, an administrator creates a certificate for the web server and has a trusted authority sign it, otherwise browsers warn users. Commercial authorities sell certificates, and a free automated service such as Let's Encrypt issues basic ones. X.509 certificates make an authority and a public key infrastructure necessary to verify the link between a certificate and its owner. That is also the weak point: if one authority cooperates or is compromised, a {{ref:sysd-found-179}} becomes possible.

sysd-found-181.title: Symmetric-key encryption: one shared secret for both directions
sysd-found-181.text: Symmetric-key encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt plaintext and to decrypt ciphertext, so both parties must hold that shared secret. Needing both to have it is the main drawback compared with {{ref:sysd-found-173}}. Its strength is bulk data. Apart from the one-time pad, symmetric algorithms have smaller keys, which means less storage space and faster transmission. Modern systems therefore agree on a fresh secret key for each session using {{ref:sysd-found-174}} or another public-key protocol, then encrypt the bulk of the messages symmetrically. No physically secure channel is needed. Stream ciphers encrypt a message one digit or byte at a time, and block ciphers encrypt a block of bits as one unit; AES uses 128-bit blocks. Popular algorithms include AES, ChaCha20 and Twofish. Encryption does not guarantee a message stays unchanged. So a separate code that checks the message is often added, and one can be built from an AEAD cipher such as AES-GCM. Session keys come from pseudorandom key generators, and weak randomness in them has led to cryptanalytic breaks, so implementations need a high-entropy source.

sysd-found-174.title: Diffie-Hellman: agreeing on a secret in public
sysd-found-174.text: Two parties can end up holding the same secret key while an eavesdropper reads every message. Diffie-Hellman key exchange is a mathematical method of securely generating a shared symmetric key over a public channel. It replaces key exchange by courier, and the key then encrypts later traffic with a symmetric cipher. Both parties publicly agree on a prime modulus p and a base g. Each picks a secret number and sends g raised to it mod p, then raises the received value to its own secret and reaches the same shared value. Only the two secret numbers stay private. An eavesdropper must solve the discrete logarithm problem, which is hard for large groups, and primes of at least 2048 bits are recommended. By itself the method is non-authenticated, so a way to check who is on the other end must be added to prevent a {{ref:sysd-found-179}}. Ephemeral keys give {{ref:sysd-found-052}}: new key pairs are generated for each session and discarded afterwards. Much Internet traffic uses groups of 1024 bits or less, and the Logjam attack exploited export-grade 512-bit groups.

sysd-found-175.title: The chain of trust from a root certificate down to a site
sysd-found-175.text: A certificate is only as good as the signature on it, and that signature has a signer of its own. A chain of trust lets a certificate be validated against its parent certificates, back to a root certificate that serves as a trust anchor. A root certificate is self-signed and has no parent. Intermediate certificates only sign other certificates and must themselves be signed by a root or another intermediate. A leaf certificate cannot sign others. To validate a server certificate, the client checks that its subject matches the hostname it connects to and that a trusted certificate authority signed it. Browsers and operating systems ship lists of default-trusted authorities set by root programs. Firefox uses the Mozilla program everywhere, while Chrome, Edge and Safari mostly use the operating system's trust store. Trust bits record each root's valid purposes, so an authority can be trusted for TLS server certificates but not for code signing. A self-signed certificate is worthless for trust between unacquainted parties, so public Internet servers need certificates from a trusted public authority.

sysd-found-178.title: Why one bad certificate authority can break everyone's trust
sysd-found-178.text: A certificate authority is a trusted third party that stores, signs and issues digital certificates, so the whole system's security depends on it. It verifies an applicant's credentials before certifying that a public key belongs to the named entity. X.509's critical weakness is that any authority a party trusts can issue a certificate for any domain. A browser trusts dozens of them, so subverting one lets an attacker impersonate any site. An attacker who steals an authority's private keys can forge certificates without further access. Publicly trusted authorities therefore keep keys in hardware security modules and the long-term root key in an offline one, signing only shorter-lived intermediates. The CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements cap certificate lifetime: 60 months from 1st July 2012, 398 Days from 1 September 2020, and 47 Days from 15 March 2029. Certificate Transparency requires all TLS certificates to be logged in publicly auditable records, to detect fraudulent ones in real time. It has largely superseded HTTP Public Key Pinning, which browsers deprecated for its risk of bricking sites.

sysd-found-191.title: RSA: encrypting with a key you can publish
sysd-found-191.text: RSA is a public-key cryptosystem in which publicly revealing the encryption key does not reveal the decryption key. So anyone can encrypt for the key's owner, and the owner can sign messages. A message is enciphered with the key its intended recipient has publicly revealed, and only that recipient, who knows the decryption key, can decipher it. Anyone can verify a message signed with the privately held decryption key by using the public encryption key. Signatures cannot be forged, and a signer cannot later deny a valid one. Encryption represents the message as a number M, raises it to a publicly specified power e, and takes the remainder when divided by n. Here n is the public product of two large secret primes p and q. Decryption uses a secret power d, where e * d is congruent to 1 modulo (p - 1) * (q - 1). Security depends in part on the difficulty of factoring n. In practice RSA often exchanges the secret key for symmetric encryption, which is better for bulk data.

sysd-found-043.title: HTTP authentication: the server challenges, the client answers
sysd-found-043.text: HTTP has a built-in way to ask who is knocking: a general framework for access control with extensible challenge-response schemes. The server issues a challenge before serving the content, and the client supplies credentials. An origin server challenges a request with 401 (Unauthorized) and must include a WWW-Authenticate header listing at least one challenge. The client answers by sending its credentials in a request header. Valid credentials that are not adequate to gain access should get 403 (Forbidden), not 401. A protection space is the server's origin combined with the realm value, so realms split a server's resources into spaces, each with its own scheme.

sysd-found-072.title: HTTP client errors: the 4xx codes you meet most
sysd-found-072.text:
A 404 is the error everyone has seen, and it is one of a family. The 4xx class says the client seems to have erred. The server should explain the error and whether it is temporary or permanent, and the codes apply to any method.

400 (Bad Request) means the server will not process the request because of a perceived client error, such as malformed syntax, invalid message framing or deceptive routing. 401 (Unauthorized) means the request lacks valid credentials and must carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge. 403 (Forbidden) means the server understood the request but refuses it, even with credentials that are insufficient.

404 (Not Found) means no current representation was found, or the server will not disclose one. It does not say whether this is permanent, and 410 (Gone) is preferred when the condition is likely permanent. 405 (Method Not Allowed) means the method is known but not supported by the target resource, and the response must list the supported methods in an Allow header. 408 (Request Timeout) means the server did not receive a complete request in time, and the client may repeat it, on a new connection if needed.

409 (Conflict) means the request conflicts with the target resource's current state, and the user might be able to resolve it and resubmit. 412 (Precondition Failed) means a precondition in the request headers evaluated to false. 413 (Content Too Large), 414 (URI Too Long) and 415 (Unsupported Media Type) mean the content is too big, the URI too long, or the format unsupported. A temporary 413 should carry Retry-After.

sysd-found-062.title: HTTP intermediaries: proxies, gateways and tunnels
sysd-found-062.text: A request rarely travels straight from browser to origin server. An HTTP intermediary is a proxy, gateway or tunnel placed between client and origin server so a request can be satisfied through a chain of connections. A message that crosses three intermediaries passes through four separate connections. A proxy is chosen by the client, usually through local configuration, and organizations use proxies for security services, annotation or shared caches. A gateway, also called a {{ref:sysd-blocks-137}}, acts as the origin server toward the client but translates requests and forwards them inbound. A tunnel is a blind relay between two connections that does not change messages, for example carrying TLS through a firewall proxy. An interception proxy is not chosen by the client but filters or redirects outgoing port 80 traffic. At the protocol level it is indistinguishable from an on-path attacker. Each proxy must append a Via header describing how it received the message, which helps avoid request loops. An intermediary that holds a shared cache is especially vulnerable to cache poisoning.

sysd-found-071.title: HTTP redirects: the 3xx codes and where they send you
sysd-found-071.text:
Sometimes the right answer to a request is to look somewhere else. The 3xx class says the user agent must take further action to fulfill the request, usually by repeating it at a different URI.

Most redirects point to another URI in the Location header: 301, 302, 307 and 308. Others offer a choice of representations (300), send the client to a different resource (303), or point to a stored result (304). 301 (Moved Permanently) assigns a new permanent URI that future references should use, and it is heuristically cacheable. 302 (Found) means the resource is temporarily elsewhere, so the client keeps using the original URI.

For historical reasons a client may turn a POST into a GET after 301 or 302. 308 (Permanent Redirect) and 307 (Temporary Redirect) avoid this, and 307 forbids changing the method on automatic redirection. 303 (See Other) is mainly used to send the output of a POST to a resource that can be separately identified, bookmarked and cached. 304 (Not Modified) means a conditional GET or HEAD would have given 200 but its condition was false. The stored representation is still valid, so no content is sent.

When following a redirect, the client replaces the target URI and drops automatically generated connection and origin-specific headers. It should consider removing headers that carry credentials or cookies for security. It should also detect and break cyclical redirection. An earlier specification advised at most five redirections, and some clients still enforce such a limit.

sysd-found-073.title: HTTP server errors: the 5xx codes
sysd-found-073.text: When a 5xx arrives, the fault is on the server's side. The 5xx class says the server is aware it has erred or cannot perform the requested method. 500 (Internal Server Error) means the server hit an unexpected condition that prevented it from fulfilling the request. 501 (Not Implemented) means it does not support the functionality needed, for example when it does not recognize the request method. 505 (HTTP Version Not Supported) means it does not support the major HTTP version in the request. Two codes belong to servers acting as gateways or proxies. 502 (Bad Gateway) means the server received an invalid response from the inbound server. 504 (Gateway Timeout) means it did not get a timely response from an upstream server. 503 (Service Unavailable) means the server cannot currently handle the request because of temporary overload or scheduled maintenance. It may send Retry-After to say how long the service is expected to be unavailable, as an HTTP-date or a number of seconds. An overloaded server might simply refuse connections instead.

sysd-found-190.title: Four extra status codes: 428, 429, 431 and 511
sysd-found-190.text: RFC 6585 defines four optional status codes, 428, 429, 431 and 511, for common situations that less precise codes handled poorly. Clients treat an unknown code as the generic code of its class. 428 Precondition Required says the server requires a conditional request, typically to avoid the lost update problem. That is where a client GETs a resource, modifies it and PUTs it back while a third party changed it. 429 Too Many Requests says the user sent too many requests in a given time. 431 means the request headers are too large, and 511 means the client must authenticate for network access.

sysd-found-077.title: HTTP caching: answering a request without asking the server
sysd-found-077.text: The fastest request is one that never reaches the origin server. An HTTP cache is a local store of earlier responses, with the subsystem that controls their storage, retrieval and deletion. It reuses a prior response to answer a later request, which cuts response time and network bandwidth. Using a cache is optional in HTTP, but reuse is the default when nothing prevents it. So the rules focus on stopping a cache from storing a response that is not reusable or reusing a stored one inappropriately. The cache key is at least the request method and target URI. Many caches store only GET responses and so key on the URI alone, while the {{ref:sysd-found-065}} adds request fields to the key. Most commonly a cache stores a 200 (OK) response to a GET. On a miss a cache can collapse several incoming requests into a single forward request, reducing load on the origin server. It must write unsafe requests through to the origin before replying, and such requests may invalidate stored responses.

sysd-found-079.title: HTTP cache freshness: how long a stored response stays good
sysd-found-079.text: A cached copy has a clock. A response is fresh while its age has not exceeded its freshness lifetime, and a fresh response can be reused without contacting the origin server. Lifetime is the time between the origin generating a response and its expiration time. Age is the time since the origin generated or last successfully validated it, and a response is stale once age exceeds the lifetime. The primary mechanism is an explicit expiration time from the origin, using the Expires header or the max-age directive. A cache takes the lifetime from the first matching rule: s-maxage for a shared cache, then max-age, then the Expires value minus the Date value. When none exists, the cache may assign a heuristic one, only for heuristically cacheable status codes or explicitly cacheable responses. It should use no more than some fraction, typically 10%, of the interval since Last-Modified. The Age header carries the cache's estimate of seconds since the origin generated or validated the response.
